title: Cotangent surjectivity and graded dimensions detect complete local isomorphisms
statement: Let $(C,\mathfrak m)$ and $(D,\mathfrak n)$ be commutative Noetherian local rings [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring] complete for their maximal ideals [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion], so $C\cong\varprojlim_{j\geq1}C/\mathfrak m^j$ and $D\cong\varprojlim_{j\geq1}D/\mathfrak n^j$. Local means having a unique maximal ideal. Fix identifications of both residue fields with a field $k$ [def-weil-field]. Let $f:C\to D$ be a local ring homomorphism inducing the identity on $k$, where local means $f^{-1}(\mathfrak n)=\mathfrak m$. Assume its induced $k$-linear map $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\to\mathfrak n/\mathfrak n^2$, $c\bmod\mathfrak m^2\mapsto f(c)\bmod\mathfrak n^2$, is surjective. Then $f$ is surjective. If in addition, for every integer $j\geq0$, the finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces $\mathfrak m^j/\mathfrak m^{j+1}$ and $\mathfrak n^j/\mathfrak n^{j+1}$ have equal dimension, then $f$ is an isomorphism. Here each vector-space structure is induced by the corresponding residue-field identification and dimension is the cardinality of a basis.

source.place: Tag 06GZ (lemma-surjective-cotangent-space), conditions (1)-(2); ring-theoretic graded-dimension argument in Tag 07XH (lemma-approximate-versal), proof after the dotted-arrow construction. The latter is extracted as a base-independent ring lemma. See literature/stacks-project/artin.tex for the second cited proof.

proof.text: Put $J=\mathfrak mD$, the ideal of finite sums $\sum_i d_i f(c_i)$ with $c_i\in\mathfrak m$. Locality gives $J\subseteq\mathfrak n$. Cotangent surjectivity says that for each $y\in\mathfrak n$ there is $c\in\mathfrak m$ with $y-f(c)\in\mathfrak n^2$. Thus $\mathfrak n=J+\mathfrak n^2$.

source.place: Tag 06GZ, lemma-surjective-cotangent-space, implication (2) to (1); absolute cotangent calculation.

proof.text: The $D$-module $M=\mathfrak n/J$ is finitely generated: Noetherianity gives finitely many ideal generators of $\mathfrak n$, whose classes generate $M$. The previous equality gives $\mathfrak nM=(\mathfrak n^2+J)/J=M$. The Jacobson radical of $D$ is $\mathfrak n$, since it is the intersection of its unique maximal ideal. Apply the cited Nakayama lemma with $R=D$ and $I=\mathfrak n$ to obtain $M=0$, hence $J=\mathfrak n$.

Apply the complete-source surjectivity lemma to $f:C\to D$ and $I=\mathfrak m$. Completeness of $C$ supplies $I$-adic precompleteness. Since $ID=J=\mathfrak n$, completeness of $D$ supplies $ID$-adic Hausdorffness: an element lying in every $\mathfrak n^r$ maps to the zero compatible sequence and is zero by injectivity of the completion map. Finally $C\to D/ID=D/\mathfrak n$ is surjective, since the residue-field map is the identity on $k$. The cited lemma therefore makes $f$ surjective, proving the first assertion.

source.place: Tag 06GZ, lemma-surjective-cotangent-space, completeness passage; Mathlib complete-source lemma replaces the inverse-system exactness passage.

proof.text: Assume now equality of all graded dimensions. Surjectivity of $f$ and locality give $f(\mathfrak m)=\mathfrak n$: any preimage of an element of $\mathfrak n$ lies in $\mathfrak m=f^{-1}(\mathfrak n)$. For $j\geq1$, write an element of $\mathfrak n^j$ as a finite sum of products of $j$ elements of $\mathfrak n$ (absorb each ring coefficient in the first factor), and lift every factor to $\mathfrak m$. This proves $f(\mathfrak m^j)=\mathfrak n^j$; the case $j=0$ is surjectivity of $f$. Thus $g_j:\mathfrak m^j/\mathfrak m^{j+1}\to\mathfrak n^j/\mathfrak n^{j+1}$, $[x]\mapsto[f(x)]$, is surjective. It is well defined since $f(\mathfrak m^{j+1})\subseteq\mathfrak n^{j+1}$, and $k$-linear since $f$ induces the identity on the residue field.

source.place: Tag 07XH, lemma-approximate-versal, graded-dimension argument after the dotted arrows; explicit maps on associated graded pieces.

proof.text: For each $j$, set $V=\mathfrak m^j/\mathfrak m^{j+1}$, $W=\mathfrak n^j/\mathfrak n^{j+1}$ and $K_j=\ker(g_j)$. The quotient-dimension lemma makes $K_j$ finite-dimensional, since it is a subspace of the finite-dimensional space $V$. The maps $K_j\hookrightarrow V\xrightarrow{g_j}W$ give a short exact sequence: the first is inclusion, the last is surjective by the previous step, and its kernel is precisely the image of the inclusion. Apply dimension additivity to obtain $\dim_k V=\dim_k K_j+\dim_k W$. The assumed equality $\dim_k V=\dim_k W$ implies $\dim_k K_j=0$. A zero-dimensional space has empty basis and hence is zero. Therefore every $g_j$ is injective.

source.place: Tag 07XH, lemma-approximate-versal, equal finite lengths imply injectivity; here dimension additivity is applied directly on each graded piece.

proof.text: If $x\in\ker f$, induction gives $x\in\mathfrak m^j$ for every $j\geq0$. The base is $\mathfrak m^0=C$. If $x\in\mathfrak m^j$, its class is killed by $g_j$, so injectivity of $g_j$ gives $x\in\mathfrak m^{j+1}$. Hence $x$ has zero image in every $C/\mathfrak m^j$. The injective completion map in the definition of completeness gives $x=0$. Thus $f$ is injective and surjective. Its inverse respects addition, multiplication and the unit by applying the injective map $f$ to the corresponding identities, so $f$ is a ring isomorphism.

source.place: Tag 07XH, lemma-approximate-versal, final inverse-limit isomorphism argument, written as a kernel induction.
